subject: Snapshot purge & backup erase — traceability, TTL and visibility

Subject: Questions on backup purge and deletion visibility for audit

Hi Vivek,

Quick question from our audit team: when a data-deletion request (legal erase) is applied to a primary dataset, how and when does that deletion propagate to backups / DR snapshots and cross-region replicas? Specifically we need:

- A clear timeline (best-case and worst-case) for when the deleted object is removed from:
  - incremental snapshot chains,
  - offsite replicated snapshots, and
  - long-term archive (if applicable).
- Which internal artifacts we can provide as evidence (snapshot manifest IDs, tombstone markers, GC logs) and their retention windows.
- Whether a jurisdictional legal hold (e.g., EU GDPR subject access with retention override) prevents the usual purge, and how that is represented in your logs.

We have a scheduled regulatory review next week — any concise summary or a short runbook snippet we could attach to our binder would be ideal.

Thanks,
Jane Smith

Hi Jane — thanks for the clear list. Short answer up top, then details below:

Summary (high-level):
- Deletion from the primary is recorded as a tombstone and included in the next incremental snapshot.
- Garbage collection that physically removes data from immutable snapshot blobs typically runs on a configurable cadence (default: 30 days) and can be accelerated via an erasure job for regulated requests.
- Cross-region replicas follow the same tombstone propagation semantics; depending on replication lag, worst-case propagation to all regions is typically 2–72 hours.

We’ve attached our internal erasure workflow diagram and the customer-facing backup policy PDF for your binder. I’ll loop in Rishi and Marissa for the exact artifacts you can extract for evidence.

Quick notes on the audit artifacts you asked for:
- Snapshot manifests: we can provide manifest IDs and the chain relationships (manifest -> snapshot ID -> object listing).
- Tombstone logs: our GC writes tombstone markers with object IDs and timestamps to the audit topic retained for 180 days by default.
- GC runbook / job traces: successful GC job runs include start/end timestamps, bytes freed, and list of manifest IDs compacted.

If you need a formal statement for legal, let me know; otherwise we can produce the manifest & GC job trace for a sample erase request you provide.

Thanks,

Adding technical detail for evidence and timeline (pinging operations runbook IDs):

- Snapshot mechanics: incremental snapshots reference object blobs by content ID. A delete in the primary creates a tombstone entry (object ID + delete_ts) which is included in the next snapshot. Until GC compacts and removes the blob, older snapshots still reference the blob (but it is logically deleted).

- GC cadence & acceleration: default compaction window is 30 days. For erasure requests tied to legal obligations we support an accelerated compact (manual approval + schedule) that will run a targeted compaction across affected manifests. Expected wall-clock for targeted erase: 24–96 hours after approval (depends on data size and region).

- Cross-region: replication is asynchronous. Tombstones are sent through the same replication pipeline; typical lag is minutes, but if bandwidth constraints exist at replicate time it can extend to a few days. We track replication offsets per-region and can provide offset timestamps as evidence.

- Evidence artifacts we can hand over:
  - snapshot_manifest_ids.txt (list of manifest ids touched)
  - gc_job_<id>.log (start/end, freed bytes, manifest compaction results)
  - replication_offset_report_<region>.csv (offset timestamps)

- Legal hold behavior: when a hold is placed we mark the related object IDs in the retention control plane and GC excludes them from compaction; holds are visible in retention_control.log with hold_id and scope. Holds can be narrow (single tenant) or broad (jurisdiction).

I’m including the internal runbook path for the run that produces the artifacts: https://drive.redwood.internal/runbooks/backup-erasure-flow (restricted access). For customer-facing evidence, we typically provide the manifest IDs and the GC job trace (redacted as needed).

—Rishi
Principal SRE, Redwood Inference

Hi Jane — following up with an actionable set you can include in your regulatory binder. We can deliver the following within 48–72 hours after you confirm which erase request(s) to use as examples:

Deliverables we will provide:
- snapshot_manifests.txt — list of manifest IDs with creation timestamps (shows tombstone inclusion).
- gc_job_trace.zip — GC job log (start/end, freed bytes, compaction results).
- replication_offsets.csv — per-region replication offsets and timestamps.

Typical timelines to include in the binder (language you can copy/paste):
- Tombstone creation: immediate at time of request.
- Logical deletion visibility in snapshots: included in the next incremental snapshot (minutes–hours).
- Physical removal from snapshot blobs (after GC): default 30-day compaction window; targeted legal erasure: 24–96 hours after approval.
- Cross-region propagation: normally within minutes–hours; worst-case (bandwidth/queue backlog) up to 72 hours.

On legal holds: if NovaCorp places a jurisdictional hold, we will exclude the affected object IDs from GC and flag the holds in the retention_control.log. Holds must be communicated to us in writing and we will provide the hold_id and retention_control.log excerpt as evidence.

Next step: please reply with either the sample object IDs / request ID you want us to use, or confirm that we should choose the most recent 3 delete requests for your tenant and produce redacted artifacts. Once you confirm, we’ll open HS-45219 and push the artifacts to a secure drive link for your audit team.
